t: Minimize the Maximum of Two Arrays — Binary Search + Inclusion–Exclusion
o: We choose disjoint sets of integers: arr1 avoids multiples of divisor1, arr2 avoids multiples of divisor2. For a candidate cap x, count how many integers in [1..x] each array can draw from: good1 = x − ⌊x/d1⌋, good2 = x − ⌊x/d2⌋, and usable-by-both = x − ⌊x/d1⌋ − ⌊x/d2⌋ + ⌊x/L⌋ where L = lcm(d1,d2) (inclusion–exclusion). Feasibility requires good1 − both >= uniqueCnt1, good2 − both >= uniqueCnt2, and good1 + good2 − both >= uniqueCnt1 + uniqueCnt2. This predicate is monotone in x, so binary search. Example 3: d1=2,d2=4,L=4; at x=15, good1=8, good2=8, both=7 → 8−7=1... careful: numbers divisible by neither (odd non-multiples handled) give exactly enough — answer 15.
k: Binary search on the answer x; feasibility is monotone.
Inclusion–exclusion with L = lcm(d1,d2) counts integers divisible by neither divisor.
Three counting conditions cover both individual quotas and the disjointness requirement.

a.n: Approach 1: Binary Search on Cap with Inclusion–Exclusion Counts
a.i: feasible(x): let a = x − x/d1 (ok for arr1), b = x − x/d2 (ok for arr2), ab = x − x/d1 − x/d2 + x/lcm (ok for both). Need a − ab >= u1, b − ab >= u2, a + b − ab >= u1 + u2. Find the smallest feasible x by binary search over [u1+u2, ~1e18]. Counts fit in 64-bit since lcm <= 1e10 and x up to ~4e18 — use unsigned/128-bit care in C++ or cap hi at 1e18 which suffices given quotas < 1e9 each.
s: Define feasible(x) with the three inclusion–exclusion conditions.

w: Overflow is the main hazard: lcm up to 1e10 and mid up to ~2e18 demand 64-bit (and hi must not overflow when computing mid — use lo+(hi-lo)/2). JavaScript loses integer precision near 1e18; Number is still adequate here since the true answer is < ~4e9·something small, but BigInt is the rigorous choice. Deriving the three conditions (especially the joint quota a+b−ab) is what interviewers probe. Follow-up: three arrays with three divisors — same technique, more inclusion–exclusion terms.
